utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We seem to be full house today. I see that the witness is not yet in the courtroom. Is that a signal that there are preliminaries? Yes, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. I don't think preliminaries, but we have the exhibits to clean up. We will do it in the order the Court desires.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So let's call the case first.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. All right. Let's finalise -- let's finalise the exhibit business relating to the witness we finished with yesterday. You will have noticed, in the meantime, that we have Judge Kwon missing this morning. He is away with the president and others today. He will be back with us on Monday. So we are invoking, of course, the provisions of Rule 15 bis. Yes. Now, documents that the Prosecution wishes to tender with the testimony of PW-130? Yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, just before the mentioning of the exhibits regarding this witness, I would like to mention to the Trial Chamber that I received the translation of the document 5D142, 5D152 and 5D153 that I presented to the witness 131 during the cross-examination. I want to inform you that the translation into English is in the e-court system and I would like to ask you to admit these documents into the file.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. That was the previous -- not this last one we finished yesterday, the previous one.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right, Mr. President. It was the previous witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I remember we had left three documents in limbo. So these three documents, it's 5D142, 5D152 and 5D153, which were marked for identification only when they were tendered, have now reached maturity age and will be admitted as full documents. Full exhibits. Thank you. So let's now go to PW-130. Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. First, which I think we've already dealt with is P02313 which was -- I'm sorry, we didn't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 2313 is the testimony, his previous testimony in Krstic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. 2314, the pseudonym sheet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Now these two will both go under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Now, running through the contents of the packet which was passed out, the intercepts, 1138A, 1138B, 1138C, under seal, please. 1138D, also under seal. And 1138E. That is tab 1. Next, 1357A, 1357B, and 1357C. That is tab 2. Next, 1392A, 1392B, and 1392C, which is tab 4, and A and B under seal, please. Then 1395A, B, C, D, E and F, if I can say it that way, with A and B under seal, please. That is tab 5. Next would be P02298, 2299 and 2300, which were photographs of antennas. 2301, 2302, 2303 and 2304 which are more photographs. 2306, and 2307, photographs of tape recorders. 1925, although that may have already been -- that has not been tendered. 1926, again photographs. 2315, which is handwritten intercept notebook number 231. 2316, which is handwritten notebook number 98. And then we have PIC 00055 and 56, which were photographs marked by the witness in court. And, Your Honours, what you should also have and the Defence, which I passed out at the end yesterday, is an index to the packets to make it a little bit more easy to navigate what the different versions are. This includes tab 3 because it is in the packet which had already been passed out, but as I said at the beginning, that was an error. That was not one of the intercepts by 130.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you so much, Mr. Nicholls. Any objections from any of the Defence teams? Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We do have an objection, Your Honour. First of all, to maybe to do it in an organised fashion with respect to Exhibit P 02298, 99, 300, 301, 302, 303 and 304, as well as P 02306 and 2307, including P 02315 and 2316 we have an objection. This was not produced to us in the past and, as reflected in the Prosecutor's very own confidential exhibits to tender list, that does not bear a 65 ter number, so we are objecting on that basis. With respect to the other exhibits, if I may, we do have an objection to the inaccurate and non-specific translation that was performed with respect to the English translation, specifically in P 01138, identified as the 65 ter number 1138A, and 1138D. Further on, P 01357, identified as 65 ter number 1357A. P 01392, identified as 65 ter number 1392A and then Prosecution Exhibit P 01395 identified as 1395A and 1395C. Your Honour, all of us believe, as the Prosecutor himself said yesterday, on page 57, lines 22 through 23, that although he tried to dissuade the CLSS section to interpret the words from the logbook and instead to translate those words, we insist that those specific documents be translated, not interpreted, the way perhaps CLSS believes they should be interpreted or the way the Prosecutor believes they should be interpreted. We believe that the documents, especially those which are not only perhaps significant but important in this case, should be given again to the CLSS and that the Court reserves its right. And I know they are marked only for identification because we have our pending motion with respect to the chain of custody of those issues, but that we get a very clean copy with respect to those specific translations. There are errors that we believe we do not just bring out for the Court; some we did in the translation, but there were additions made on it and of course they were innocently made we think by the CLSS. But nonetheless, for the Court to have a complete record and to ensure that our clients get a fair trial, we think that those exhibits should not be introduced into evidence at this time, but rather tendered back to CLSS, so that they can do a proper translation and not interpretation of those very exhibits. Therefore, we object to those specifically, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. For the time being, I will not ask for other objections from other Defence teams. One moment. I'll ask Mr. Nicholls to address this objection, which seems to be divided into two types of objections. Yes, Mr. Nicholls or Mr. McCloskey; I don't know who is going to deal with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: First, Your Honours, 2298 and onwards, the photographs, those we sought to put on the exhibit -- on the -- those were disclosed by EDS back in April, I believe. It turned out that there had been a problem, that a surrogate sheet was put on EDS, that was brought to our attention by Ms. Fauveau recently. We printed out copies of that. I think there should have been an objection made at the time I was showing them to the witness and we could have dealt with it then, rather than having no objection whatsoever to me having them marked, put in. But there has been no prejudice whatsoever from that. The witness identified those photos, the Defence had plenty of notice in advance that I planned to use those exhibits. They were on my list from early on, so I think the objection is untimely and there is no prejudice whatsoever. The photos I think are helpful in showing the type of equipment that was used and this is a type of objection that should be made earlier, when the evidence is shown to the witness or when it's put on my list and there is a complaint. So I think this is just a little bit too little too late. There has been no prejudice and it's untimely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Does that -- I can understand that to refer to 2298, to the photographs of the various antenna and to photograph of the tape recorder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But does if also apply, what you just stated to 2315 and 2316, in other words, the two handwritten intercept notebooks?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I didn't -- I don't have it on my screen, but yes, that is correct. I'm not sure there was an objection to the notebooks. There was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, there was of course. I mean the objection was on the same basis. I just want to --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It applies as well. Those have clearly been part of this from the beginning; they have been available to the Defence. And it's the -- it's the -- those are helpful to the Court because those are the originals of the photocopy that we are putting in. So it's the same documents. Those were disclosed on the 16th of June, 2005. And again, they were on my list to be used from the beginning. I think it's -- my response is the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, the other category of documents objected to, namely the 1138, 11 -- 1357, 1392 and 1395, what's your position on --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I believe Mr. McCloskey wants to address you on the translations issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, Mr. Ostojic and I have, I think, in the past, spoken briefly about CLSS's efforts to -- in translation sometimes they do a little analysis like the case I remember here, I don't know which exhibit it is, but they put in the village I think it's Caparde or Pasarde which is an actual village as opposed to the indistinguishable word that was in the notebook. As I mentioned, we have been talking with them about that and as these -- if -- as we notice these things happening and as counsel notices them, we'll try to -- I think we will probably agree on most of these and I think we can -- before these intercepts actually get finally offered, I think we can have those problems all worked out among ourselves. We are just -- point out the ones they are most concerned with. There are some 2 to 300 of these intercepts and we have got two or three months to work them out. So I think between us, we can work this out. But CLSS is just trying to be helpful. There is nothing really very prejudicial in them, but counsel is correct, these are unlike some other documents. They should really stand for the words that are there and they -- we shouldn't really have a lot of analysis like that from the translation unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's deal with this. Mr. Zivanovic, let me finish, please, with Mr. Ostojic's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we agree that, again, these categories -- these exhibits or documents do indeed fall into two separate categories and need more or less to be treated differently, somewhat differently, according to their specificity. The thing is and we are in agreement on this, I think the admission of documents is so vital to any case that I wouldn't even dare start discussing it with my two colleagues present here in the absence of Judge Kwon. I think it's a matter that each challenged document must be thoroughly discussed between all of us and a decision taken by all of us, preferably unanimously, because, as I said, each document may be vital to the case. So I will start with 2298, 2299, 2300, 2301, 2302, 2303, 2304, 2306, 2307, 2315, 2316. These -- yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, could I make one more point, please, on the notebooks. 2315 and 2316, which is that the Defence actually asked that those be used with the witness, asked that he be shown them and asked that he flipped through them so they also made use of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That happens with many challenged documents. You don't need to address that. We have been dealing with such problems, if you can call them problems, all our legal lifetime. So don't worry about that. These documents, you did not also mention 1926, didn't you, which is another photo?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour, because that number does bear a 65 ter number. But if I can just add in the proper framework for just one minute, Your Honour, I think the onus is not on the Defence in order to advise the Prosecution during their case in chief when they should or should not follow the Rules of Procedure and Evidence that are prescribed in this Tribunal. And secondly, we are not to advise them during their case in chief whether they should or should not follow the rules handed down by yourself, Mr. President, in identifying documents and giving us those documents. Instead, I think failing to do so should not be something that they should argue that we were waived during the process. We did not waive the right. We think the procedure here was to allow the Court to hear the evidence to allow those exhibits and then we are going to have a debate about those exhibits. If in fact the rules have changed and the Court would like before a witness testifies for us to go through each exhibit and set forth our objections to those exhibits, we will be glad to do it. But I think the failing to do so should not, and it's misguided with all due respect to my learned friends, to suggest that we have waived. In fact, they have failed to follow not only the rules of the Tribunal, but also this Court's order when and whether or not they can produce documents. And they could have asked for leave of court, but they failed to do so, not that the Defence failed to make an objection in a timely manner. We believe the objections are, in fact, timely when we bring them up when the Court instructed us earlier how to proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ostojic. All these documents that I have referred to will, for the time being, be marked for identification purposes, pending further deliberations by the Trial Chamber in due course. Now, coming to 1138A, 1138D, 1138 -- 11 -- 1357A, 1392A, 1395A, 1395C, these are all intercepts. More or less, we have already given you a clear cut indication that since intercepts are all being challenged, basically we will be marking them for identification for the time being until the matter is determined. Probably the matter will be determined in the course of the proceedings and not at the end of the proceedings. But for the time being, these that I have mentioned, together with the others that were not mentioned by Mr. Ostojic, will be, for the time being, marked for identification purposes only and then we'll ultimately decide whether to admit them at all at a later stage. All right? That disposes of the Prosecution documents. Now, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I also have an objection, Your Honour, linked to the documents submitted by the Prosecution. Of course, in addition to the general remarks that have already been heard in the proceedings and about which the Trial Chamber will rule, I would like in particular to indicate that I oppose to the admission of Prosecution numbers 1395E and 1395F. This is an intercepted conversation dated the 2nd of August, 1995 at 1300 hours. And on the list, it is indicated that it is an audio tape. We did not hear the audio tape here. We heard a CD or a DVD, I don't know exactly which. Secondly, it is not indicated here that it is a copy, and it is not indicated what the source was, what the original from which the copy was made. So I think an erroneous decision could create an erroneous impression that we are admitting an original audio tape. Furthermore, when an original audio tape has not been produced in open court, and also in view of the fact that the other party has it and has listened to it together with the witness as the witness has confirmed in the proceedings, I think that the admission of such evidence would be undermining the integrity of these proceedings, because what this Chamber should know, they should know exactly whether this is the original and whether the copy that is being tendered corresponds to the original, especially in a situation when someone is challenging it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. I think again there are two aspects to this. The first point made by Mr. Zivanovic, I think, was covered by myself when I was dealing with the intercepts challenged by Mr. Ostojic, the same argument or the same reasoning applies. With regard to the second point made in relation to whether this is an audio or audio tape that's a copy, whether it's not, I think it will remain a submission for the time being and we will -- I don't know if Mr. McCloskey or Mr. Nicholls want to intervene now, but I don't think that it's in our powers to say any more on it than what Mr. Zivanovic has. I don't think we ought to say anything on it. We will take it as a submission made which will be considered later when we weigh the pros and cons or the plus and minuses in admitting this document or not admitting it. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honour. I think that's fine. There are just a few of these audio intercepts that we have and we can deal with that. I would just point out that the witness authenticated the recording that we heard in court, that it was the same and it was the one that he had heard on August 2nd and transcribed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Incidentally, Mr. Zivanovic, you don't seem to have asked the -- or expect or demand from the Prosecution the production of the original audio, do you? We had an indication from Mr. -- I don't know who, I think Mr. McCloskey, two days ago that the original is in the vault, so it is available. I understand it was made clear. I don't interpret your objection as amounting to a request that the Prosecution bring forward this original audio. I didn't understand you that way any way. I understood you as objecting to the tendering of what we have here, what the Prosecution is seeking to tender. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct. I made an objection here, among other things, to the admission of what the Prosecutor has tendered. However, even back then, I wanted clarification, and when the Prosecutor offered to show me the tape in the Office of the Prosecutor, I understood you to say then that that can be done only in this courtroom. If the Court -- if the tape needs to be heard at all. And I relied on that. I think that was perfectly appropriate, and I have no interest in listening to the tape on my own. My interest is in having the tape heard in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The objection or the point with the Prosecution at the time, it's you, and of course, it was rather unusual, unorthodox, to hear suggestion that it be played to you privately and not to everyone here to be able to follow. I mean, because others may pick up things from it that, upon which they can build arguments in relation to other intercepts and other recordings. So we do not give instructions to the Prosecution on what documents or what exhibits to bring forward. It's up to you. All right. So the position as it is now, it seems that you are objecting to 1395E and F, on the basis of what you explained. Your objection being countered amongst other things by the Prosecution saying that this was -- this tape copy was confirmed as authentic by the witness. So we leave it at that. It will also be marked with the rest of the 1395 sections of that document, marked for identification and we will later on decide on the admissibility of that document. All right. Any other objections in relation to the proposed documents to be tendered by the Prosecution? I hear none. So the rest are so admitted. Now, there are some documents which I understand the -- some of the Defence teams would like to tender. The Popovic Defence team made use of several documents. Do you wish to tender any of them?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have submitted a list of those documents, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I will go through it myself, then. It's 1D82, 1D83, 1D86, 1D93, and then 5D146, paragraph 4, subparagraph 1, which will need, of course, to be given a different number. Now it will be 1 -- I don't know, 1D, 5D, I don't know how you would --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, 1D5D146.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one small correction. I said, speaking of 5D146, it was not paragraph 4. It was page 4, subparagraph 1, because the record says paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's paragraph 4 and may have been my mistake. It's 5D146, page 4, subparagraph 1, subparagraph 1. Whatever that means, subparagraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is precisely the passage marked by number 1 and it's at the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. I think it will be clear from -- any objection from anyone, Prosecution or other Defence teams? Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour, just one point. We didn't receive the list which would be nice to get in advance if they are sending it out, a courtesy copy. And second, just in terms of the statement and the subparagraph, I also think it's more helpful just to put the whole document in rather than paragraphs of a document so that the context is clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I make it clear that, particularly in relation to this statement, we object to that vigorously. We relied on the fact that only that part of the statement was cross-examined in by my learned friend, Mr. Zivanovic. And, Your Honour, were the whole of this statement to go in, it would really change the goal post quite substantially.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are fully in agreement that it should be only this subparagraph from this document that will be tendered by Mr. Zivanovic on behalf of his client. Now, yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, our position -- you made your decision is that the whole document should come in when it's so short, it's just a few pages, but otherwise, I don't see any reason for just the subparagraph to come in because, again, he read from it, he quoted it and he made his record pretty clear on the record, so I don't see any reason to put in just a subparagraph of a document like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it's quite clear why we should actually, in the circumstances, but that's the position. May I ask, Mr. Zivanovic, to refresh your memories? 1D82, 83, 86 and 93, are they still without a translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, unfortunately I think we don't yet have a translation, but it will probably be available by the end of the day. In fact, no, no, it's not certain when we will have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation] Same as we do have a translation in e-court, 5263.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of which document?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Document 1D83 is the same document as 5D153.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you agree with that? I mean, I can't confirm or deny. But usually Madam Fauveau is correct, most of the time. I don't want to give you --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will have to check again, Your Honour, but I don't think that's the case. I think it was 1D83.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's play it safe. I would rather not take risks. These four documents, 1D82, 83, 86, 93, will, as we have done in the past with other documents, and hitherto untranslated, will be marked for identification and will become full documents, full exhibits, once we have confirmation that the translation has been completed as -- and introduced in the records. As regards 5D146, it's only subparagraph 1 on page 4 indicated by Mr. Zivanovic that will be admitted. Now, would anybody else like to tender documents in relation to the testimony of PW-130? Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a document 5D150.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And is it translated?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any objections? So it is so admitted. I understand that the Nikolic team also had an intention or -- no, no, but that's -- I see the Nikolic team here, but it is 5D150. It's obviously a mistake. It should be the Miletic team. Yes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, Your Honour. I think 1D94 has been omitted, although it was used in cross-examination. It was not included in the list. So with my apologies, I would kindly ask you to tender that. It's dated 4th August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Any objection to that? We did not have it on our list. So 5D -- sorry, 1D94 is also -- is it translated, Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, but it has been given to the CLSS along with all the others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It will be treated just like the others have been treated. It will be marked for identification purposes only for the time being, and then once the translation is made and introduced in the records, we will upgrade the document to an exhibit. That concludes the tendering procedure in relation to PW-130. There doesn't seem to be any further business to transact. Let's bring in witness, Major Rutten, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Major Rutten, and welcome back.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are going to proceed with the cross-examinations and hopefully finish today. I think there was only one or two cross-examinations left. Three? There is Madam Fauveau. Who else?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: There's two and a half, Your Honour. I think Ms. Condon and then Madam Fauveau and then me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Who wishes to go first? I think it was Ms. Condon who was going first upon our request, actually, so -- yes, go ahead, Ms. Condon, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Major Rutten, I want to take you back just briefly to the evidence of Monday in relation to -- I asked you about some meetings that took place at Potocari with Muslim leaders. You recall that?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Perhaps if the witness could be shown P 02103, Your Honour. It's photograph 7. You have that photo in front of you?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Perhaps if Madam Usher could assist with the -- if the witness could mark this photograph. Now, just before I proceed, is this a better photograph than the one that I showed you on Monday?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Mark the house, you're able to do that with this photo?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Okay. So perhaps could you mark, if you can identify from that photo, the house, houses or the area of where these meetings took place?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: All right. Now I'll get to you initial that, please.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: What initials do I --

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Your initials.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Okay. [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: All right. Now can you -- how many meetings took place at that house?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: The exact amount of meetings, I don't know. Exactly, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Can you give me an estimate?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: A rough estimate could be six or seven times.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And in what period did these meetings take place?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: In the period throughout February until June.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: No meetings in July?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: No, no meetings in July.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: All right. Now, I've concluded with that photo. So perhaps if that photo could be saved, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Registrar. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Now, I also asked you some questions on Monday in relation to the second role of film that -- from which you had taken photos. You recall those questions?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And in particular, there was a reference in your Assen debriefing statement to having taken photos of some Muslim leaders. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Now the Muslim leaders that you took photographs of, are they the two gentlemen that we referred to on Monday, Mr. Mandzic and Mr. Sabanovic?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Now, I presume that you took those photos in your capacity as an intelligence officer; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: You didn't take them for our own personal reasons?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: All right. Now, knowing that these photographs were on that second roll of film, why didn't you hand over that second roll of film to the Dutch Ministry of Defence?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: They never asked for it.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: But, Major Rutten, you obviously appreciate the significance of the roll that you had as an intelligence officer, the information gathering role, you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: So you telling me that simply because they failed to ask for that, you didn't have the wherewithal to hand over that?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: No, sorry. I have to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, one moment. Mr. Nicholls. Mr. Thayer, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. This ground was covered on Monday with respect to questions that were or were not asked about the film that was or was not turned over and the expectations that Major Rutten had about being asked certain questions and not being asked certain questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He did go into details and he explained how he told them that he would eventually hand down the other film and how actually he handed it within our 24 hours or within -- even mentioned the time and to whom he handed it when he was eventually asked to hand it over. So why go over the details again?

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Your Honour, just in my submission, that's not correct what the learned Prosecutor said. I did not ask any questions about the decision not to hand over the second roll of film.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You just asked him why didn't you land over the second roll of film to the Dutch Ministry of Defence?

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: But these questions haven't been asked before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course they have been answered before. Of course they have been answered before. He went into great detail because this matter was dealt with pretty thoroughly.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: May I proceed, Your Honour, in relation to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But not asking the same question again.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Now, you also indicated, Major Rutten, that in relation to the second roll of film, that it referred to happenings in and around Potocari on the 12th and 13th of July. That was your evidence on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Well, can you be a little bit more specific, please, because I didn't ask you that. What do you mean when you say that those photographs related to happenings in and around Potocari on the 12th and 13th of July?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Those photos that I already gave to this Court in the Krstic case were the photos with the detailed photos that I had of 12th and 13th July and that were, for instance, the photos of the pile of IDs burning and that I took from the compound in Potocari in front -- in the picture that was in front of the "White House".

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yes. But you mentioned seven or eight photographs around the period. We don't have seven or eight photographs in this trial that -- of photographs that you've taken.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: No, but they were offered to me in the Krstic case and it's not my obligation, I think, that which one are offered to this Court or not or in which trial or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: No, no. I appreciate that, Major, but the fact is is that in particular -- well, in particular, on this second roll of film, were there any photos in relation to observations of the role that DutchBat was playing insofar as the transport of the refugees were concerned? Any photos of that nature on this second roll of film? I didn't ask you that on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: No?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Those pictures were only on the first roll.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Right. Well, now that we are on this topic of the role of DutchBat in terms of the transport of the refugees, it's your evidence in this trial, and in Krstic, is it not, that at no stage were the DutchBat soldiers working with the refugees at the point where the men were being separated from the women; is that correct? Perhaps, shall I read out a particular part of your summary in this trial --

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: -- just so that you understand what I'm referring to. This is at page 47, Your Honour, lines 23 to 25, and this is at the point where you and Lieutenant van Duijn have your difference of opinion. Yes?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: All right. "He told this to Van Duijn who had a different point of view. On the other side of the line at the buses, Serb soldiers were carrying out the separation of men from their families. UN soldiers were not working with the refugees at the point where the men were being separated from the women." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: That's your evidence?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yes? And is it the case that you have always, Major Rutten, maintained that position that at no point were DutchBat in any way involved with assisting or collaborating with the separation?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: You haven't, have you? You've had a different view point about that, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, I had a different view point, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Right. Well, you're on your oath in the Krstic trial, as you are here. So you're telling the truth to this Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yeah? So on those occasions where you've had a different point of view, has that not been the truth?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let me explain. It's being put to you that while to this Trial Chamber you have indicated that to your knowledge that DutchBat personnel were at no time involved in separating the two genders, men from women. In other instance, and it's as I understand Ms. Condon, she is referring to your testimony in the Krstic trial, you did not exactly say so. You maintained a different position. She is actually suggesting to you that if what you have told this Trial Chamber, as you say, is the truth, what you may have told another Chamber, that's the Krstic trial, may not have been the truth. This is what is being proposed to you. Did I put it right?

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Half right, Your Honour, if I can be so bold.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Perhaps if I actually specifically put to Major Rutten the other occasion that I am referring to. It's the case, is it not, that you were interviewed in August of 1998 by Nova television?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And that was a controversial television interview?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: The subject -- the ramifications of it were controversial, you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yeah. And the reason why it was controversial, was it not, was because in the context of Lieutenant Van Duijn's actions, you accused him of having collaborated with the Serb soldiers in the process of separation of the men and the women, is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yes. So you were telling the truth, were you not, when you were interviewed by the Nova television?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yes? And it's clear, in that context, that in your mind, there was no doubt that the DutchBat were assisting in the process of the separation of the men and the women?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Now are you making a total different point because I had a -- I was arguing with my colleague about what he was actually doing on the road, and that looked like collaboration. He had a different point of view on that. And I tried to explain to my colleague what he was actually doing at that point, and you are saying something completely different, to my view.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Alright. I'll rephrase it, then, Major Rutten. Is that -- is it the case that the view you expressed on Nova television in August of 1998, that the DutchBat were collaborating insofar as the separation of men and women are concerned, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: No, no. You're rephrasing it again. And you are saying something different than what I am saying at the moment. I'm only saying that the Lieutenant Van Duijn, at the way he worked on that road, he didn't realise what I saw through the image through the camera from the photos that I made on there and that is the position that I had. And I tried to convince my colleague at that point what that picture looked like. That is the only thing I explained. And that looked like if we were taking part in evacuation of the Muslim population.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: But correct me if I'm wrong, did you not at some stage as well, when you were interviewed by the NIOD report, specifically the way it's presented, is that you accused Major -- Lieutenant Van Duijn of aiding and abetting in relation to this process of separation. Is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: You are saying that I am accusing him. I never accused him. I said only that he --

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: All right. I'll move on, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. But aiding and abetting is a very precise legal term with its own legal connotations.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: I appreciate that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And if you are suggesting that he accused him of aiding and abetting, I think you need to face him with chapter and verse.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: I'm reading from -- I don't have it on the e-court, Your Honour, but I can read from the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: I'm reading from part 4, chapter 4, section 28 of the NIOD report. We've already established you're familiar with this document.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: I haven't got all lines in my mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: But Major, you were interviewed for this report?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, in 2000, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And there is a specific chapter that's headed "Suspicions and Dilemmas," Van Duijn and Rutten. You, no doubt, have read this chapter?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, years ago.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Let me remind you of a specific aspect of it. This appears at the bottom of page 2. Page 2, "It was clear to Rutten what fate awaited the men since the discovery of the bodies and his visit to the "White House". He tried to convince his colleagues of this and demanded that they cease to assist the deportation. Rutten in particular found that Van Duijn went too far in his attempts to appease the VRS troops and was engaged in 'aiding and abetting.'" Now, is that information that you provided to the NIOD report, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: It is information that I provided, but I never used those words that are mentioned there.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Aiding and abetting?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: That's their interpretation?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yeah, it's a historic report, so they are using their own terms. They are not to my --

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: But we have established, just to make it clear, that you used the word "collaboration" in the Nova television programme?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yes. And not only that, you indicated on Monday that the management report presented some difficulties for you in terms of providing a completely candid account of what had gone on in and around Potocari on those two days in July. You recall that?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And part of the reason for that was that you had some personal difficulties about incriminating fellow soldiers who may find themselves exposed to criminal proceedings should you give a full account; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: I explained that on Monday, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: But what I'm suggesting to you is when it came to the time to provide -- to give this interview to Nova television in 1998, would it be fair to say that you didn't have those same concerns, insofar as Lieutenant Van Duijn was concerned?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. That's improper question. That's irrelevant to this witness's testimony. He's answered this version of the question four or five different ways and this is not helpful to the Court respectfully, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Agreed. Yes, objection sustained. Let's move on to something different, Ms. Condon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, sir, if I may say something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You don't need to say anything for the time being, only what you are asked and when you are asked, Major Rutten. Be patient with us.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: May I proceed, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Major, I want to just take you back to this question of the intelligence that you received prior to your mission to Srebrenica. You indicated on Monday that you did in fact receive names of officers from both sides that you were expecting to come into contact with you. You recall that evidence?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yeah? And no doubt -- well, obviously, that means that you received names from officers from the VRS; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Some, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yeah, some. In particular, no doubt you were informed in advance as to the relevance of the Drina Corps in terms of the area that you were going into?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yeah? Well let me ask you this: What particular names did you receive?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Last week, you heard one name, Jovic. There was in the northern part Nikolic, in the southern part, we had to deal with a man called Colonel Vukovic. These are some names I do recall now.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: That you received before you went there?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: The ones that you were told these are people that you would be expected to deal with?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And in particular, I want you to focus your mind on -- in the intelligence area, because obviously that was something that was complementing your role. What names did you give -- were you given in so far as the intelligence functions?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: I don't recall those names any more. No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: You just have no memory?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: What about the security functions of any individuals within the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: No, I have no recollection.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: No?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: What about the name Popovic? Was that ever --

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: It never came up.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Then?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: No. But it has subsequently?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, during --

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: We'll get to that. Now, after your debriefing, and I don't propose to go through the same questions again. What I want to ask you is this: Is that it's unclear to me from your evidence on Monday whether or not you were specifically asked, in your debriefings from the Dutch Ministry of Defence, to provide any information that you had gleaned as an intelligence officer. Because I'll just give the references. At page 45 -- I'd ask my learned friend before he objects, Your Honour, that I can give the page references.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll wait to see the references. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: At page 45, lines 10 to 15, I asked you, "Were you not asked to provide in those debriefings any information that you had gleaned as a results of being an intelligence officer?" And your answer was, "Yes, I was asked to, but the problem was we had almost no photos whatsoever." That's one answer. And then at page 47, lines 1 to 8, I put to you, "But you agree that were you in fact questioned to provide information in relation to the intelligence that you gathered from your time in Srebrenica to the Dutch Ministry of Defence?" And your answer was, "There were no specific questions, as I remember, on specific intelligence matters themselves." So, perhaps, just can you clarify for me, were you asked questions or not? It's a simple matter, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it was a simple question that was asked on Monday and he answered it quite simply. I think we are just wasting time going over old ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He has already -- I mean -- I don't know what you feel about it. He explained on Monday how poor intelligence was, how poor intelligence was. He's explained also and to what extent he was an intelligence officer and he has explained what questions were put to him and what answers he gave. What else can we get from this?

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, with respect, in my submission, it is unclear from those two sets of questions and answers. It's a simple question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But it's a repetitive question. You asked this question and others asked this question before. So next question, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: When you -- I'm going to return to some answers that you gave in relation to your proofing session, Major Rutten, with Mr. Harmon, the Prosecutor in the Krstic trial. You indicated that how it was that these videos and then photos were shown to you were that you had asked about some people that were still in Serbia. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yeah? And your specific evidence was that you asked, where were they at the moment and you and Mr. Harmon talked about that. You recall that?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yeah? Now, these -- obviously these weren't people generally that we are talking about, were they, they were specific names that came up?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Names were never mentioned. That was the thing I told on Monday too, about the photographs.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: So your -- what you're saying is that you did not specifically mention any names, but Mr. Harmon then said to you, that you might be interested in some pictures of people?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: I explained this on Monday already.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: But there must have been hundreds of people that you would have seen in that period in and around Potocari on those two days; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes. I see, daily, hundreds of people.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: So no names at this stage came up between you and Mr. Harmon; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yeah? But you indicated just before that the name Popovic did come up at some stage.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, but you asked that question in relation to something else.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: You asked that question just before about my period during my mission in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: So now you're, to my opinion, you're relating something --

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: -- totally different.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Or you have to ask me another question.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: I haven't asked --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please don't argue with counsel, please. If you want to make a submission to the Trial Chamber in relation to any question, you're free to do so. You have every right to do so and we'll direct you. But, please, no -- don't engage into a direct confrontation and argument with Defence counsel, who is doing her job here. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: So in relation to this process with you and Mr. Harmon and the people that you were still interested in, is that a fair assessment, that you were still wanting to know if these people were still in Serbia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: That question didn't came up. He came up himself because he heard about my plan to go abroad for a new mission, and that was his -- so he said, okay, then I have to talk to someone else. He spoke on the phone to someone else and he never gave any names.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: But what about you? At any stage, did you identify particular people that you said, well, is such and such still in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: No, never?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: No? Was there any discussion at all about -- from Mr. Harmon, about people that might be of interest in the context of the Krstic trial, people that the Office of the Prosecution were still interested in investigating?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: I told you on Monday that I tried to establish some -- some Serbs from the video stills that I saw and that is the only thing I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: All right. Now, in relation to the video, we've already established that when you saw the video, you made no identification of anybody; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yeah. And what you said to me on Monday was that after you'd seen the stills from the video, that Mark showed you a book of photographs. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And from that book of photographs, you made an identification?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Is that right? Now, just before we get to the book of photographs, what you've indicated today is that in the course of your mission in Srebrenica, the name Popovic was a name that was familiar to you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes. During my mission, yes, it was told once we spoke about the name in the battalion.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: All right. And when that name was spoken of, it's correct, is it not, that that was in the context of the function that that person performed? I'll rephrase that. That was clumsy. That when his name was spoken of, you were made aware of whether or not what area he was in, whether or not it was intelligence, whether or not it was in security; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. We never made the -- we had a very poor intelligence situation in the battalion as well and they said these are familiar names to us and they never made a relations to the functions those persons had.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Is that a serious question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In what context was his name -- did his name come up or was mentioned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was one of the known names on the Serbian side and that's the only thing I heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was just objecting to the question put to the Major Rutten by my learned friend.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: I withdraw that; it was a comment.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: You keep on, Major Rutten, emphasising this poor intelligence.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yeah? You no doubt consider yourself to be a professional about what you do?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: You take pride in your job?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yeah? You've been what promoted -- what rank were you when you were in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Lieutenant.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And you're now a Major; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yeah? So I take it from that that you would not be proud, if somebody were to accuse you of not being a good intelligence officer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is wasting time, it's irrelevant, and, frankly, it is getting argumentative and disrespectful to Major Rutten.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: That's not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's move to the next question. Because who wouldn't? Who wouldn't?

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: With respect, Your Honour, this witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please don't argue, Ms. Condon. Move to your next question. It's almost a facetious question that you put to Major Rutten. Please, your next question.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Play I proceed, Your Honour, in so far as the relevance has come about by this witness indicating the poor intelligence. May I pursue that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course you can pursue that. You can just ask him one simple question, what do you mean by that? And we'll see what he has to answer. But incidentally, do you intend to refer Major Rutten to any allegations made by others that he fell short in his duties or performance as an intelligence officer?

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then why did you ask the question? That's why I told you it was a facetious question.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Major Rutten, just in relation to this issue about the poor intelligence that you seem to rely upon insofar as the DutchBat was concerned, was that due to the personnel or what was the reason for that?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: We received almost no information; in fact, none whatsoever through the UN chain of command in referring intelligence at all. The only intelligence we had and that's also in different reports, was what we had in the line of our sight. So that's why we tried to patrol to the borders of the enclave because then it was in our line of sight somewhat further to have any view of what was happening just around the enclave. We didn't hear nothing, nothing at all during our whole period.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Let me put this to you, then: What you say, just so that I understand it, is that in the context of this name that you received of Popovic, you received that without any information as to what position this person held; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: I already answered that question.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: I'm just -- so it's fair to say, is it not, that insofar as intelligence is concerned, that's a useless piece of information?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: No. I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'll sit down, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Now, just going back to this book of photographs that we were talking about before, that Mark Harmon showed you, can you just give me an indication as to how many -- can you recall how many photos were in this book of photographs?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: No. A lot, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: M'hm. And do you have any recollection of whether or not, prior to looking at the photographs, there was an index provided as to the photos?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: I only saw the photos.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: M'hm. Perhaps if I could have some assistance from Madam Usher, Your Honour. Perhaps, could you have a look at this, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We need to see it too. Put it on the ELMO, Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Just the first page to begin with. No, no. Just the first page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you remove the plastic cover, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: You see that, do you, Major?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yes? Now, is this the book of photographs that you were shown in your proofing session with Mark Harmon?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: No?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: No?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: I only saw the photos. I never saw a written text. I only saw photos.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: If you just flip over to the next page, please. Was -- just so that we make sure, if you open up that, that wasn't part of the book of photographs that you were shown?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Okay. Perhaps if we can move on, then, and flip to number 1, please. Is this now the book of photographs that you were shown?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yeah, could have been one of them I was shown. I don't know exactly if he was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's make this clear. What Ms. Condon is obviously after, whether you were just shown a photo or whether you were shown also a photo with the name or an indication of the name of whoever is supposedly shown on the photo in any characters, Latin or Cyrillic. Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, maybe I missed it, but if Major Rutten could have an opportunity to flip through the binder, that might help this procedure along just a bit.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: He can do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We need to know that, whether the photos you saw -- you were shown, had the name superimposed or whether they were just clean photos of an individual and you were asked whether you could identify them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those were the photos without names I saw.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: All right. Just so that we establish this, it's the same photo book - don't get rid of it yet - it's the same photo book, but without, you say, the index at the front, that we saw on the ELMO before? Perhaps if that could be shown again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think we need to waste time like this. He has already said that he never saw any writing.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Just tell me, Major, underneath tab 6, how many photos are there?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Two photos.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Two photos. And one of those photos is the photo from which you've made an identification in this trial; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yes? And that second photo that's under that tab, that formed part of the same photo book that you were shown in the Mark Harmon proofing session; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want to know, please, when you made that identification of that photo, was it the case that you said to Mr. Harmon, "Oh, yes, that's similar. That looks like the man that I saw outside the 'White House,' that's similar to the man that I saw outside the 'White House'"?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: I don't know whether I've used those words that you are saying now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What do you remember saying to Mr. Harmon? There is the whole thing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember that I said those are the men that I probably saw at the"White House".

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Thank you. Probably saw. Because the fact of the matter is, is that when -- so you're not sure about that, if you say that's probably who I saw -- Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, my learned friend has the answer from the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: She is perfectly entitled to ask him whether he's sure about his assessment or not. So please proceed with your question, Ms. Condon.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you -- go ahead. It's your question. I'm not going to repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: When you say that you said that's probably the person that I saw, that's because you're not 100 per cent sure that it was?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: That was my first answer then. You asked me what I said to Mark Harmon. That was my answer then to Mark Harmon and later on by flipping again through the photos, looking again, looking again more clearly, I identified that man that was on the photo.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Right. Okay. So it took you a number of processes before you did?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: By flipping again, that's not a number of processes. By flipping again, just what I said.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go back to what happened on the 28th of November, which is last Tuesday, in the proofing session with Mr. Thayer, because the fact of the matter is, is that when you were first shown this photo that you have in front of you in that proofing session, your words were to Mr. Thayer, "I cannot be certain if I recognise him now." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yes. And, again, I'd suggest to you -- you don't have to agree with it -- that that's because in the same way that you first saw it, you said that's probably the man, it's because you simply cannot be sure that the man in the photo is in fact the man you saw outside the "White House"?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: I'm not agreeing with you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: All right. So let's go to this person that you say that you saw outside the "White House".

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm about to move to a final topic. I see the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's what we will do. We'll have -- you still have about one hour or 45 minutes, Ms. Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And Mr. Haynes?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Ms. Condon has covered very much of my cross-examination. I don't think I'll have more than 10 or 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we'll have a 30-minute break, then. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Condon, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Major Rutten, I was just turning to the question of this person that you say you saw outside the "White House". Now, we've already gone through in considerable detail about your activities in terms of this second visit to the "White House". You recall that evidence on Monday?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Now, if the witness could be shown P1535, please. Now, that's a photo in front of you, of the "White House"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Now, perhaps if Madam Usher could assist the witness. The first event that you gave evidence about on Monday was that you saw two Dutch soldiers stationed outside the "White House"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: I'd like you to mark on there, please, where those Dutch soldiers were.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Right. Now, when you arrived, we've established that you walked around to the left side of the house; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yeah? And what about Major De Haan? Where was Major De Haan on this second occasion to the "White House"? Because remember that we've established that although you had forgotten that he was in fact the -- I reminded you that in his statement he said he was there on the second time.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Is that funny? You smiled then. Is that funny, is it?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Sorry, I don't understand that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please, Ms. Condon and Major, your question again, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Could you please mark where Major De Haan was?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: I cannot mark that because Major De Haan was in front of the compound just at the opposite of the "White House".

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: All right. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One question, because that X that you've marked may be a little bit insufficient to explain to us the exact position of the two Dutch soldiers. You put an X there. How -- can we have more or less an indication of the location. How far -- what's the distance to -- to the building itself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the road to the building it's almost 30 metres, I think. And there were the soldiers who were standing. It's not on the road, the paved road you see. There is not a paved road behind the fence and there were the two soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think that explains it better.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Perhaps the X that you've marked now was the way the two Dutch soldiers were; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Perhaps, could you just do DS to -- next to this so that we know, initials DS for Dutch soldiers?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: All right. We've then established that you walked around the house to the left side; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yeah? So is that the left where the aerial -- the tower is, yes, and then you went to the back of the house?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yes? And then you went back to the front of the house which is when you saw the balcony filled with the refugees; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: All right. I want you to mark for me the point where you were at -- exactly at the front of the house where you saw the balcony filled with the refugees.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: All right. And we established that that all -- that process that we've just gone through, in your evidence you said on Monday, took about 15 minutes, you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yeah? This is on the second visit to the "White House". And then you've said that you spoke to the two Dutch soldiers about the deutschmarks being forced. You agree with that?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
