utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In the middle paragraph in English, you've stated, and I quote, [In English] "I see the big picture. We are also a part of it because we were on positions where we could be taken hostage. We had seen it in the previous period. And then I saw that Krajina was overrun by the Croats, in the meantime, heavily armed by the Americans. And then I saw that the English silently left Gorazde. The situation was such that there was no possibility of a good peace agreement. Eventually it did come." [Interpretation] Sir, were you under the impression that the fall of Srebrenica was a consequence of a political agreement?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer. One moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just in order to make sure that the transcript does indeed reflect what Madam Fauveau read, there is a mistake in lines 11 and 12 of the transcript that says "the situation was such that there was no possibility of a good peace agreement." While the text says exactly the opposite, the situation was such that there was a possibility of a good peace agreement. Yes, Mr. Thayer. That's for the record, but I suppose Mr. Thayer --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. President, that was the first reason for my rising. The second one is with respect to the answer which we are being shown here, I think it would be helpful to place it in the proper context in which that answer was being given, which is the question on the prior page. And I think once that is done, it will be clear that this answer that is being shown here is irrelevant and frankly is not -- is not being fairly characterised or tied to the Srebrenica enclave and its fate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it's a clear cut question that is not really dependent on what the previous statement of Major Rutten on that occasion was the result of or a consequence of. I think there is a simple question. He is being asked, I don't know how and to what extent he can answer it, but Major Rutten, were you under the impression that the fall of Srebrenica was a consequence of a political agreement? Do you know anything about that? Can you give us an answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The moment I gave that statement in the van Kemenade report --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Forget the other statement, please. Let's concentrate on this question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. It was not -- at that time I was in the enclave, I could not make such a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Conclusion.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Conclusion, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And have you changed your mind since then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Later on during the van Kemenade, we had more news on TV and then the puzzle for me, at least, was clarified that there were a lot of steps made on the political scene that there was a situation, that we were on a position that was not the best position to be in in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Major. Yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Madam Fauveau. Mr. Haynes now will be the last Defence counsel to cross-examine you. Go ahead. I don't know how long you anticipate cross-examining the witness. We need about four, 2, 3 or 4 minutes for the tendering of the documents and I don't know if there is going to be re-examination and I haven't asked my colleagues whether we are putting questions to the witness. So basically, do you anticipate re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I don't believe there will be any, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Yes, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we were given a report from the witness last Friday after we concluded our cross-examination and it was my understanding, obviously, we want to wait to see what other questions are asked, that we would be given the liberty to ask questions limited in their nature that was not included in the report, since we didn't have the benefit of the report during our cross-examination. So we may have some but we will be able to inform the Court accordingly once the cross-examination is concluded by my learned friend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mr. Ostojic. Provided we conclude with this witness today. Yes, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Major Rutten, just to ground the next few questions that I'm going to ask you, you were at the base at Potocari between Monday the 10th and Friday the 14th of July, that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And during that period of time, you were both in the compound and outside and you patrolled fairly widely?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: That's also correct, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And during that period of time, through your various functions, you received sources of intelligence and information from those who you were working with?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: That's also correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'd like, if I can, pretty briefly, to try and place into a time frame, and ask you to clarify, some of the incidents that you witnessed and were aware of, okay?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: At some stage during that time period, you saw some Serb militia looting houses. Can you help us as to when that was?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: The question that -- the question that was asked earlier was that there were civilians looting the houses near the compound, and I don't recall that I said Serb militia was looting the houses. Serb militias were looting our personal belongings behind the bus remise, I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, in that event, Serb civilians looting houses. When was that? That's really what I want to know, when it was.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Later on in the evening, at the 12th and 13th, 14th and so on, the days afterwards, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You also saw some dead bodies [Microphone not activated]. You also saw some dead bodies and I think you've told us that that was in the afternoon of the 13th of July. You'd agree with that, would you?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And you also saw a pile of personal effects being burned and I think you'll agree that that was on the 14th of July?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes. It already started on the 13th but it was still burning on the 14th, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Was it on the 14th that you took the photograph that we've seen?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you also went to a house where men were being held. Did you only go to one house?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you go to houses on more than one day?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: During the night, during the 12th and 13th, I visited several houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, what I'm interested in is whether you went to one house or more than one house where men were being questioned.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: In the "White House", the men were being questioned. In some other houses near the road on -- if you're standing with your back to Srebrenica, on the left-hand side of the road, there were some other houses where men were held, but there were a lot of Serbs around so we couldn't enter that house -- those houses. Other houses we checked but there were no Serbs or Muslim men around in that -- in the other houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I hate to labour the point, but did you visit a house other than the "White House" where men were being questioned?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And you were not aware that any other house was being used for men to be questioned?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes. We were aware of that but we, as I said before, we couldn't enter them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. You also saw the screening of military-aged men. Did you see that on one day or more than one day?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: I saw that on more than one day.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And was the screening of men taking place in the same place -- at the same place on those days or in different places?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: In different places.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The reason I asked you about these events, these are all events that you photographed, you've told us.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Not all of these events that I just told you about. It wasn't always possible to photograph freely.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: You took these photographs I think with your own personal camera, a Fuji 35 millimetre?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: You only had one camera, did you?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And your experience was it was easy to load, easy to use?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Consistently produced good photographs?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Do you recall now what size of film you were using, 24 exposures, 36 or what?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, as I understand your evidence, you used two separate films during the period we are talking about. Do you recall now when you changed the film?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: No, not exactly, but during the -- during the 13th.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You said this morning, when you were being

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: photographs of Muslim leaders. I assume you took those before the 10th of July when you were working in the enclave.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: I want to understand, please, the development of these films. There were only two that failed to be developed in late July of 1995, were there?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: No. I had some more films but there were also personal films from colleagues on the compound, and also some films about the photos that I made of the Muslim leaders were also on another roll than the two you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Right. But you had two films which concerned the events of the 12th and the 13th?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And the 14th?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: I'm not clear what you did with them. Did you hand them over, both of them, to your superior officers in Holland?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think, at least in my mind, it is clear because he's told us exactly what happened with one and with the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: With respect, this is the first time we've heard that there were more than two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. I understand your question to be limited to the two films that go to the 13th, 12th, 13th and 14th, in other words, the events that were unfolding during those three days. This is how I understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'll put one simple question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If I have misunderstood you, then of course please correct me and put the question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: When being cross-examined by Ms. Condon this morning, you told her that the photographs of the Muslim leaders came from the so-called second roll. Is that right or wrong?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: That is wrong, because the Muslim leaders were on the first -- were on another roll because they couldn't have been on the second roll because I made them earlier, together with other photos, and they didn't belong on the second roll of -- they couldn't be on the second roll because I made them much earlier. But the total package of photos I had later on, that's true, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: That's why I asked you the question, because it appeared to me that you had developed a photograph from way before the 11th of July and the only other photographs that you had back came from the 14th of July and I wondered how that could be but you have now explained it. There were more than two films. The photographs that you received back - I know this is very difficult and I know you have been asked a similar question - but how many were returned to you in total?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: I don't understand your question. Which photographs are you referring to now?

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: From the two rolls which you submitted to your superiors for development.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the record is clear as to the fate of the rolls he brought out of the enclave with him. I don't think it could be any clearer than it already is in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Right, but the question is basically somewhat different. How many or which of these two rolls were, if at all, returned to him? This is the question and he can answer that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. The -- there is one roll that I never got back. That is that I gave to the Major De Ruiter. The other roll I never handed in. I also told that before, because I let them develop myself because there was never asked for. And that was I -- what I stated earlier as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Thank you. In fact, what you said earlier was that you had seven or eight photographs that related to Potocari. I wanted to know how many you got back in total. It was a full roll?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, a full 36 roll. Is that the question?

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: That's it. That's why I used the phrase "in total."

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Now, you handed the film over on the 24th of July and a day later you had a conversation with commander Bloemen [phoen], didn't you?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: The context of that conversation was such that you believed that he had seen the films or the film fully developed, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes. It was my understanding then on what he said that it could have been the case, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And you're the best evidence we're going to get on this. You loaded the films, you took the photographs, you took the film out, you handed it over. You have the conversation with Mr. Bloemen. Your understanding of the position is that that film was deliberately destroyed.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: I cannot say that because I -- I have no evidence on that. But I have some thoughts about that but no evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Well, you had a conversation with commander Bloemen in which he talked about the implications of these photographs. Did you think he'd seen them?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: So they, to your understanding, had been developed?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: That was my understanding because of what he said, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Well, I'm asking you as you sit there now, do you think that roll of film was deliberately destroyed?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: I can't say that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think he's answered that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'll leave it there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer. I suppose that your objection would have been exactly the same as I would have.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: The photographs that were not developed, you didn't think they looked very good, did you?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: I explained that earlier.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Well, you thought they didn't show the whole picture. What did they show?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: They did show the whole picture and the whole picture was that led to the discussion with my colleague Van Duijn.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Did you have doubts about Mr. Van Duijn on the 12th and 13th of July?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, your objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is territory we have covered in great detail, the encounter between Major Rutten and then Lieutenant Van Duijn. It's been asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes, would you rephrase the same question using the word reservations instead of doubts?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Did you have reservations about the actions of Mr. Van Duijn during the 12th and the 13th of July?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let him answer the question. I know that he has given --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's in Mr. Thayer's hands. This witness can come back tomorrow if he carries on like this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please answer the question. Mr. Thayer, let's see what the witness can tell us in conclusion on his colleague Van Duijn.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I said before, looking through the camera I saw a situation that didn't look very good, and then I went to my colleague and I said, or at least I tried to convince him that he -- what it looked like through the camera. And it looked like if we were assisting in evacuating the refugees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let me put the final question on this and we can move to something else. Between having doubts about Lieutenant Van Duijn, having reservations about Lieutenant Van Duijn and having a disagreement with Lieutenant Van Duijn, which one would best describe your attitude towards him at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My attitude was from a somewhat older colleague to convince him that he is -- he was putting himself to an awkward position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we can leave it at that and move to something.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes, I've got two questions that follow on from that and they really will be two questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: One of the things, in fact, probably the main thing that concerned you about Mr. Van Duijn was that on the morning of the 13th of July, he took an initiative in organising the evacuation of people at Potocari, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: You can best ask Van Duijn himself because I wasn't directly present, only the Lieutenant Koster was around then and he tried -- he spoke with Lieutenant Van Duijn.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Well, I don't want to unnecessarily call up documents, but do you recall saying to the van Kemenade inquiry, that on the morning of the 13th of July, Mr. Van Duijn organised your colleague saying, shall we begin, the sooner we start, the sooner we finish, before any Serb officers got there?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, and that was what he explained to the -- my colleague, the Lieutenant Koster and we discussed that later on and that's what -- that's how I learned about this situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And did you not consider the organisation of the evacuation to be part of your duty pursuant to a UN order?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Well, then I am going to have to ask you to have a little look at a document. It's 3D50, page 25. And in the interests of the economy of time, would you be happy just to read that in English, Major Rutten? It's the large paragraph at the bottom of the page. It's the first sentence, Major Rutten. Would you read it to yourself.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: "The orders of Lieutenant Koster and these orders came from the UN as well, were to provide support for the transport of refugees. What does that mean?"

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: That's all I want to you read. I want you to think about my last question again. Did you think it was a UN order that you assisted in the evacuation of the refugees?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: It wasn't a direct UN order. It was something that came down from the Lieutenants on the ground and later on Major Franken clarified that but we hadn't -- we had to provide support. And support means to get the humanitarian aid to the refugees that were around but not assisting, and that's something else, to my opinion, in the evacuation of the refugees.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: In acting in the way he did on the morning of July 13th, was Mr. Van Duijn acting alone or was he receiving support from other soldiers within your battalion?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: He was -- he had a part of his platoon around.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: What was the attitude of the members of your platoon towards the Muslim fighters by the 13th of July?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: My platoon was divided amongst the other platoons. I had the antitank platoon, but I was --

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: I'm going to interrupt you. I asked you a bad question, then. I meant what was the attitude of the members of the Dutch Battalion generally towards the Muslim fighters.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: There were -- I don't know -- I cannot answer this question because I don't understand it.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Well, were any of the soldiers upset with the Muslim fighters?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Not the ones that I came by, near Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: You weren't aware of people who were aggrieved about having property stolen?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: The property, the people that were -- or the persons of my group that were losing their personal belongings were aggrieved because that happened by Serbs. So that's the reason what I said I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: I'll move on. Were you aware of any members of your battalion who had been kidnapped by a Muslim fighter?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Not at that stage, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: How widely was it known by the 13th of July that private Rensen had been shot and killed?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: It was known by the whole battalion.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And you believed he had been shot in the back of the head with a dum-dum bullet, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: That specific as you are now -- we weren't aware of but that he was shot, that was clear, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Just a couple more questions. I'm going to make this a brief one lest I get accused of asking you something that's been asked before. But in 1998, when you were interviewed by Mr. van Kemenade, just before you went on the Nova television programme, you were heavily critical of some members of your battalion and the role in which they played in the evacuation of refugees from Potocari, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Are you still heavily critical of the members of your battalion and the role they played in the evacuation of people from Potocari?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: What I stated then is still my position now.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: You're still heavily critical of them?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: I have answered that question.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Mr. Ostojic, do you have any further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I do, Your Honour, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How long.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: A couple minutes, five at most.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please, can you make it two minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sure, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I can direct your attention, sir, to Exhibit 3D50 and just so we can move quickly, page 28 of that document, when it's shown here. Sir, on November 30th, I asked you for my learned colleague on page 50, lines 3 through 21, issues about illegal trading and black marketing and here in this report ... [French translation coming over English channel] ... and in this report here, that's dated the 19th of August, 1999, you have an interview. And in that interview, in the second or lower portion of that page, you discussed three things that were potentially being investigated against DutchBat III, namely, the issue of running people over, providing assistance to the Serbs in the evacuation process, in Potocari, and three, into the issue of money transactions and so on. Sir, does this help refresh your recollection as to what money transactions were being investigated against DutchBat III after the fall of Srebrenica in 1995?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes. The money transactions refer to the situation, that during the periods of leave of DutchBat soldiers, some were contacted by Muslim men to take money along to Holland and that could have been picked up later with them at home by members of the family or someone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And isn't it true, sir, that these Muslim people were giving DutchBat personnel, DutchBat III, the money stuck in coffee bags or coffee containers, do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that, but I was aware that was something that was happening and we saw that as a serious risk for DutchBat soldiers and their families.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, can you list for me, sir, in your answer here, when you say some of them would prefer things not to be stirred up, others would bear responsibility -- would want an investigation. Can you list out for me, sir, who in your opinion, were the people who would not prefer to have things stirred up and who were those that, in your mind, bear responsibility for some, if not all of the three illegal activities that DutchBat was accused of?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer, it's a compound question.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: In the interests of time, I could break it down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's suggest -- let's see if the witness can answer it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Frankly, Your Honour, it's irrelevant to the subject matter of Major Rutten's testimony before this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's put it like this: Can you very briefly pinpoint the responsibility that Mr. Ostojic is referring to on anyone in particular, without going into details, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I cannot, because I don't know who was behind it -- that the management report -- and that was in fact the thing that got put away in a drawer. Who did that and if there is something known to that and it's in the NIOD report, I think, and it's not of my knowledge now.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. Isn't it true though that even if your colleague did do something wrong, you wouldn't be able to testify against them, correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think he needs to answer that question. He's been very critical from Karremans downwards, several of his colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: With all due respect, Your Honour, I would insist on that answer or have him see page 11 of -- page 15 of that same document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Answer that question. Is there any obstruction that is in the way to criticise any of your colleagues?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. It wasn't then and it isn't now.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me turn to page 15 of that same exhibit, 5D -- 3D50, page 15. Sir, on the bottom of that page you why asked a question, in this same conversation on the 19th of August 1998, and I just want to have this to have a full understanding. In answer to a question regarding a hopeless situation, you answer, "And then even if your colleague did something wrong, are you prepared to tell it? I don't know. I don't think so," is your answer. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: I'm reading the piece out in what context I said that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Context is in whether it was the case of instituting or collecting evidence for criminal investigation or prosecution purposes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was the reason, and I stated that before, that I asked the Kodak team to put it in a kind of report to investigate that matter thoroughly.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, I know you've had some criticisms about some of the reports and investigations that have gone through. I want to just -- if you could explain to me your answer on page 11 of the same exhibit, 3D50. If we could just turn to page 11 quickly and you say it as follows, sir, and I'll just read it and have -- maybe you could help me with this. In answer to some questions, you state: "If the same people investigate the case again and again, then you are not very impartial as an organisation." With respect to that, sir, is that your belief and is that the criticism that you have of the investigations with DutchBat III?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: This question came up by van Kemenade because the same men of the military police were investigating in about three times, I think, the situation about the film roll and that was the reason I said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And one last question, if I may, Your Honour. On page 29 of your recent document that we just received ... [Microphone not activated]. On page 29 of the same document, sir, you talk about a minister striking -- you say it is "striking to realise that the minister suddenly takes -- suddenly talks a lot about career protection." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Which minister was strikingly starting to talk a lot about career protection for DutchBat III personnel?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What's the relevance of this, Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I think it goes to relevance not only of his testimony, but all of DutchBat, if there is evidence here to suggest that the ministry was seeking to somehow shape their testimony in any way, I would like to know who the minister is and, in fact, if he was giving them career protection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, first of all, that is not a fair implication from this answer that Major Rutten gave and it's irrelevant to the subject matter of this witness's testimony before this honourable Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You can make a submission out of it and in due course, Mr. Ostojic but --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That's what I only need is the name of the minister so that I can make the submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I will not ask the witness to give the name of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is there re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No questions. Major, your testimony ends here. I wish to thank you for having come again here to finish your testimony. Wherever you're going, we wish you a safe journey back home. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's very quickly do the exhibits. May we have the lists, please, or should we leave it to Monday because we have got four pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, just a bit of housekeeping for next week. We have a number of witnesses and witness estimates. If we could get a little guidance on that, so we can end on a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Guidance on what?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, we can call four witnesses and we may not make it if Defence counsel takes the four hours on each operator witness that they are asked. I think there is a very good chance that they may not take four hours for each of these simple operator witnesses, in which case we may get left with some time that we have not used up. I think if we go for three, that's probably a pretty good average, but I just wanted to warn you that was -- that's the situation. It's so hard to estimate how long these folks will take.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If it's hard for you, you can imagine how much harder it is for us, not knowing or not having any liaison or dialogue ongoing with either of you. So let's try to conclude this. The Prosecution exhibits, you have the list. I suppose, you've been provided with a list, Defence teams? All right. Are there any objections to any of those documents? I hear none, so they will all be admitted as per the list which I am signing and handing to Madam Registrar. Then there is the Gvero Defence team. Sorry, if I'm not necessarily following the same order. There are two documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 65 ter number 63D436 and IC 54.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: None, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. They are so admitted. The Borovcanin Defence team, the ICTY questionnaire. Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: None, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So admitted. Popovic team, there are two documents with no ERN. The two photos. Yes, any objections? Without an ERN number.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: They don't have ERN numbers yet, but they will have them.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Actually, one of -- just for the record, I don't think this was done but this exhibit, which my learned friend Ms. Condon showed the witness was marked as OTP Exhibit 28 in the Krstic case, just so the record is clear. I think we have an agreement on that that it is a binder of photographs which was referred to in the prior testimony in Krstic of Major Rutten. Again, it's OTP Exhibit 28.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I think we all know which photographs these are, and therefore they are so admitted. We will resume on Monday. If you could kindly try to liaise a little bit with Mr. McCloskey as to whether we will have four or three witnesses in the course of next week, I think three would be a safer guess, a safer guess. Yes, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I apologise. We also request that Exhibits number 37 and 41 be admitted into evidence. We had used those and for some reason they didn't make it through the system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are they your own 2D documents or?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I have them as 3D37 and 3D41, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, so they are not yours. They are the Nikolic team. All right. No objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So they are so admitted. Thank you, Mr. Ostojic. I think that concludes the sitting for today. Again, I wish to thank everyone for having overstayed with us for these last seven minutes. We won't have a sitting tomorrow. We'll resume on Monday morning. Thank you.
